key_insight: Fewer than 2% of FDA‑authorized AI medical devices are prognostic, with prediction horizons spanning minutes to years — highlighting a large, underrepresented device class and emerging regulatory and ethical gaps that need attention.
problem_solved: Identifies and quantifies the scarcity of prognostic AI devices among FDA authorizations and highlights the regulatory and ethical challenges that arise as prognostic models (with varied time horizons) become more common.
method: Systematic analysis of FDA‑authorized AI device list to classify devices as prognostic vs diagnostic and to measure prediction horizons.
Characterization of regulatory pathways and discussion of ethical concerns (safety, validity over time, bias, clinical impact) for prognostic models.
impact: Alerts AI/ML practitioners that prognostic devices are rare but likely to grow, requiring careful temporal validation, clear evidence of clinical benefit, and proactive regulatory and ethical planning during model development.
visual_elements: Pie chart: proportion of FDA‑authorized devices that are prognostic (<2%) vs diagnostic/other
Timeline/histogram: distribution of prediction horizons (minutes, hours, days, months, years)
Flowchart: regulatory and ethical decision checklist for deploying prognostic AI (validation, monitoring, risk mitigation)
Icon set: key risks and considerations (data drift, bias, clinical harm, transparency)
paper_title: Authorization of prognostic AI medical devices
paper_authors: Urs J. Muehlematter, Kerstin Noelle Vokinger
